extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and patent practitioners who practice before the USPTO; OED/disciplinary observers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and sanctions governing attorney conduct before the USPTO, including what conduct violates the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility and the Rules of Professional Conduct, and the disciplinary remedies (suspension, publication, consideration in future proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over disciplinary matters pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, and 11.26.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of USPTO professional conduct rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners appearing before the USPTO are subject to the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility and the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20 through 10.112 and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101 through 11.901).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events occurring before and after May 3, 2013 invoked applicability of both sets of rules; practitioners must follow these rules when prosecuting patent and trademark matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making false declarations to the USPTO regarding reduction to practice or prototypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting or causing submission of sworn declarations to the USPTO that falsely aver that an inventor actually reduced the claimed invention to practice or that a working prototype existed when it did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False declarations that materially affect prosecution (e.g., overcome prior art) can lead to patents being issued improperly and form the basis for disciplinary action and for courts to find inequitable conduct and unenforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement in litigation alleging infringement when knowing patents were procured by false declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Being involved with filing or pursuing complaints alleging infringement when the practitioner knew or should have known that the patents in suit were procured by false declarations (including misleading claims about prototypes or their location).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited violations: Sections 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(3), 10.85(a)(5), and 10.85(a)(7). Continuing to pursue litigation under those circumstances is sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to withdraw claims after learning of falsity
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to withdraw an infringement claim after being informed by the client (or otherwise knowing) that the claimed prototype/device did not operate as asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to withdraw despite knowledge of falsity can constitute a violation of professional conduct rules (identified in the order as Sections 10.23(a) and 10.23(b)(5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serving interrogatory responses or pleadings that falsely assert reduction to practice or a functional prototype
rubrics_metrics.description: Serving responses to interrogatories, motions, or other pretrial pleadings that assert there was an actual reduction to practice, or that a functional/working prototype existed or was in a named repository, when those assertions are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such misrepresentations in discovery and pretrial filings were specifically cited (Sections 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(3), 10.85(a)(5), 10.85(a)(7)). They may expose the practitioner to discipline and support findings of inequitable conduct/unenforceability in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonably multiplying the proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreasonably and vexatiously multiplying the proceedings (e.g., by filing or pursuing meritless or misleading submissions) such that the practitioner may be held liable under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 and disciplined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court found that the attorneys knew the declarations contained false statements prior to bringing suit and awarded fees under 28 U.S.C. § 1927; OED treated unreasonable multiplication as a basis for discipline (Sections 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(5), 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(7)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Making pleadings that falsely assert prototype capabilities or provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleging in pleadings that there was an actual reduction to practice, that a prototype could receive messages and caller ID, or that a prototype was located in the Smithsonian when those claims are untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements were independently cited as violations (Sections 10.23(a), 10.23(b)(4), 10.23(b)(5), 10.85(a)(2), 10.85(a)(3), 10.85(a)(5), 10.85(a)(7)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing untrue Answers to counterclaims about a functional prototype
rubrics_metrics.description: Being involved with answers to counterclaims that untruly asserted that the inventor constructed a 'functional' or 'working' prototype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conduct was cited as violating multiple Code/Rule provisions (same sections cited elsewhere). False answers in litigation can be disciplinary grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible civil liability for attorneys' fees under 28 U.S.C. § 1927
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys who unreasonably and vexatiously multiply litigation may be held liable for the opposing party's attorneys' fees under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court issued an award under § 1927 against the respondent and other firm attorneys based on knowledge of the false declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction: suspension from practice before USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall be suspended from practice before the USPTO in patent, trademark, and non-patent matters for eighteen (18) months commencing on the date of the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension is an available disciplinary remedy for violations of the professional conduct rules exemplified in this matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is ordered to comply with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 as part of the sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 11.58 concerns conditions for reinstatement and conduct during the suspension period—compliance is an explicit term of the Final Order.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED and Director publication and notice obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at OED's electronic FOIA Reading Room and shall publish a Notice of Suspension in the Official Gazette describing the misconduct and suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order includes the text of the Official Gazette notice and requires public posting of the disciplinary decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disciplinary record in future proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of this disciplinary proceeding, including the Final Order, may be considered by the USPTO when addressing further complaints or evidence of similar misconduct and may be used in future disciplinary proceedings as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations by or on Respondent's behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past disciplinary records can be considered both to aggravate sanctions and to challenge future statements by the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural disposition relating to pending matters and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties shall file a motion with the Administrative Law Judge requesting dismissal of the pending complaint, and the parties shall bear their own costs incurred to date and in carrying out the terms of the Agreement and any Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order can include procedural directions (e.g., dismissal motions) and allocation of costs between parties.
